title: YouTube 18: 6 Heists So Bold They Look Fake (One Is Still Unsolved)
_sources:
Sources (checked 2026-11-19):
- Guinness World Records news 19 Mar 2026 "Missing: Have you seen this painting? The greatest art robbery remains unsolved": 18 Mar 1990,
  two men dressed as police buzzed in, two guards tied up and taken to the basement, ~80 minutes (motion-sensor logs), 13 works incl. Vermeer
  "The Concert" and Rembrandt "Storm on the Sea of Galilee", valued ~$500 million, reward $10,000,000, Dutch Room frames hang empty, never seen again.
- A&E "The Unsolved Heist at Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum" (2025/2026): early hours 18 Mar 1990, fake officers claimed a disturbance, guard let
  them in against policy, guards duct-taped/handcuffed in basement, left 2:45 a.m., 13 works, $10M reward, empty frames still hang,
  FBI 2015 named two suspects (both dead), nothing recovered.
- Wikipedia "Antwerp diamond heist": 15-16 Feb 2003, Leonardo Notarbartolo rented an office in the Antwerp Diamond Center (>2 years prep),
  vault: combination lock, infrared heat detectors, seismic sensor, Doppler radar, magnetic field; hairspray on thermal sensor, polystyrene
  shield, tape on light sensor; 109 of 189 boxes; >$100 million; trash dumped near E19 motorway, found by landowner next morning;
  DNA from a partially eaten salami sandwich; Notarbartolo 10 years; most diamonds never recovered.
- Wikipedia "Vincenzo Peruggia": 21 Aug 1911 (Monday, closed day), former Louvre worker, white smock, lifted it off the wall, removed frame,
  a plumber let him out; discovered next day; Picasso questioned/Apollinaire arrested; hid it in a trunk in his apartment for two years;
  12 Dec 1913 arrested in Florence after offering it to dealer Alfredo Geri (Uffizi director Poggi verified); served about seven months;
  crowds came to stare at the empty space on the wall.
- Smithsonian Magazine "The Theft That Made the 'Mona Lisa' a Masterpiece" (title -> "many say the theft made it famous").
- Louvre 2025: ABC News timeline 21 Oct 2025 (about 7 minutes, truck with ladder) - see mg/ys_louvre.
- Wikipedia "Hatton Garden safe deposit burglary": Easter weekend April 2015, down a lift shaft, Hilti drill through 50 cm vault wall,
  alarm went off 3 Apr 00:21 but police did not respond; up to GBP 14 million; six elderly men, ringleader Brian Reader 76 at arrest;
  caught via cars/CCTV, Flying Squad; sentences ~6-7 years; only GBP 4.3m recovered.
- Wikipedia "Dresden Green Vault burglary": 25 Nov 2019 ~4 a.m. fire at a power box on Augustus Bridge cut street lights; window bars cut;
  display case smashed with an axe; 21 pieces with >4,300 diamonds; at least EUR 113 million; Audi later found burned in an underground car park;
  Dec 2022 31 items returned (Berlin), 16 May 2023 five members of the Remmo clan convicted; some pieces still missing (artnet 2023).
- Wikipedia "Great Train Robbery (1963)" + "Ronnie Biggs": 8 Aug 1963 just after 3 a.m., Royal Mail train, glove over the green light +
  battery for the red light, 15 men, driver Jack Mills hit over the head, GBP 2.6 million (~GBP 48-50 million today), Leatherslade Farm,
  Monopoly with real money + fingerprints, sentences up to 30 years; Biggs escaped Wandsworth 1965 by rope ladder, ~36 years a fugitive,
  returned 2001; bulk of the money never recovered.

lines.text: Two police officers rang the bell of a museum in Boston, in the middle of the night. Eighty minutes later, half a billion dollars of art was gone.
Thirteen works, including a Rembrandt and a Vermeer. And to this day, not a single one has been found.
That's number one on this list. But first, five other heists so bold they almost look fake.
And watch closely. Because almost every one of these crews made one tiny mistake.
Number six. England, August 8th, 1963. Just after three in the morning, a Royal Mail train is rolling through the dark.
It's carrying sacks of used banknotes. Millions of them.
Up ahead, a signal turns red. So the driver stops the train.
But the signal was a trick. The gang had covered the green light with a glove, and powered the red light with a battery.
Fifteen men stormed the train. The driver, Jack Mills, was hit over the head.
They unloaded more than two-and-a-half million pounds. Today, that's close to fifty million.
Then they hid at a farmhouse. And while they waited, they played Monopoly. With the real money.
That was the mistake. Police found the farm, and fingerprints all over the game.
The leaders got thirty years in prison. One of them, Ronnie Biggs, escaped over the wall on a rope ladder, and stayed on the run for about thirty-six years.
And most of the money was never found.
Number five. Paris, August 21st, 1911. It's a Monday, and the Louvre is closed.
A man in a white worker's smock walks in through the staff entrance. Nobody looks twice. He used to work here.
His name is Vincenzo Peruggia. He walks up to the Mona Lisa, lifts it off the wall, and takes it out of its frame.
At a locked door, a plumber even lets him out, thinking he's staff.
Nobody notices the painting is gone until the next day.
Police even question Pablo Picasso. And crowds come to the Louvre just to stare at the empty space on the wall.
For two years, the Mona Lisa sits in a trunk in Peruggia's apartment.
Then he takes it to Florence and offers it to an art dealer. The dealer calls in the museum director, and police arrest Peruggia at his hotel.
He served only about seven months. And many say the theft is what made the Mona Lisa the most famous painting in the world.
And the Louvre? In 2025, thieves robbed it again. With a ladder truck, in about seven minutes.
Number four. London, Easter weekend, 2015.
Hatton Garden is London's jewelry district. And under one building sits a vault full of safe deposit boxes.
The thieves climb down an elevator shaft. Then they use an industrial drill to bore through a vault wall half a meter thick.
The alarm goes off. But no police come.
They walk out with loot worth up to fourteen million pounds.
And the gang? Mostly pensioners. Their ringleader was seventy-six years old.
Their mistake: they used their own cars. Cameras picked them up, and the police tracked them for weeks.
Most of them got six to seven years. And millions of pounds' worth of the loot is still missing.
Number three. Dresden, Germany, November 25th, 2019. Around four in the morning.
A fire breaks out in a power box on a bridge. The streetlights go dark.
Two men cut through the iron bars of a window and climb into the Green Vault, a royal treasure chamber from the 1700s.
They smash a display case with an axe.
And grab jewelry set with more than four thousand diamonds. Worth more than one hundred and thirteen million euros.
Their getaway car was later found burned in an underground garage.
But police tracked down the gang, members of a Berlin crime family.
In 2022, most of the jewels came back as part of a deal. And in 2023, five men were convicted.
But some pieces are still missing today.
Number two. Antwerp, Belgium. The diamond capital of the world. February 2003.
A man named Leonardo Notarbartolo rents an office in the Antwerp Diamond Center. For over two years, he plays the part of a diamond trader.
Below the building sits a vault with a combination lock, heat sensors, a seismic sensor, radar, and a magnetic field.
His crew beat them one by one. Hairspray on the heat sensor. A foam shield in front of the infrared. Tape over the light sensor.
Over one weekend, they opened one hundred and nine of one hundred and eighty-nine safe deposit boxes.
The haul was worth more than one hundred million dollars. People called it the heist of the century.
Then, on the way out, they dumped their trash in a forest next to the highway.
The landowner found it the next morning. Inside was a half-eaten salami sandwich.
The DNA on it helped convict the gang. Notarbartolo got ten years.
But most of the diamonds were never found.
And number one. Boston, March 18th, 1990. The early hours of the morning.
Two men in police uniforms ring the bell at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. They say they're responding to a disturbance.
The guard breaks the rules, and lets them in.
Minutes later, both guards are tied up in the basement.
For about eighty minutes, the thieves walk through the museum.
They take thirteen works. Rembrandt's Storm on the Sea of Galilee. Vermeer's The Concert.
Together, worth around five hundred million dollars. The biggest art theft in history.
The museum offers a reward of ten million dollars. It has never been paid.
The FBI later named two suspects. Both are dead.
And today, the empty frames still hang on the wall. Waiting for the paintings to come home.
So, which heist was the boldest? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to Roundhead Stories for more true money stories.
